dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Fine, thank God. How are you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أَنَا مِنْ عَدَن، بِس سَاكِنَة بِصَنْعَاء.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min 3adan, bas sakna bi Sana2a.
dialogue.english: I'm from Aden, but I live in Sana'a.

lessons.culture: In Sana'a, greetings are warm and often repeated when meeting after time apart. Using a person's first name immediately after introduction is friendly and respectful. "الحمد لله" (thank God) is always included when answering questions about health or well-being, as it is throughout the Islamic world.

exercises.prompt: A man says to you: "مَرْحَبًا". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is very formal Islamic greeting. For everyday opening, "أَهْلًا" is much more natural.

exercises.tip: "أَهْلًا" or "أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا" is the everyday Yemeni greeting reply.

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you: "كَيْفِك؟". Answer that you are doing well.

too_formal.feedback: While correct, the simpler form is much more common in everyday Yemeni speech.

exercises.tip: "تَمَام" (fine) with "الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ" (thank God) is the standard everyday response.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "_____ رَامِي." English meaning: My name is Rami.

too_formal.feedback: This structure is much more formal than the simple spoken phrase used in introductions.

exercises.tip: The everyday pattern is "إِسْمِي + name" without any other words.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Yemeni Arabic: "What's your name?" when speaking to a man.

too_formal.feedback: This is more formal. Yemeni speech uses "شْنُو" for "what" in everyday conversation.

exercises.tip: "شْنُو" is the common Yemeni word for "what"; it comes first in the question.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Where are you from?" when speaking to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: This is more formal. The simple "مِنْ وَيْن" form is what Yemenis use every day.

exercises.tip: The feminine singular ending for "you" is "ِ", so "أَنْتِ" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Nice to meet you."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written-style Arabic. In conversation, "تَشَرَّفْنَا" is much more natural.

exercises.tip: "تَشَرَّفْنَا" is a useful fixed phrase for first meetings across all Arabic dialects.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "تَشَرَّفْنَا". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: That response is too elaborate for an ordinary first introduction.

exercises.tip: "وَأَنَا كِمَان" (me too) is especially easy and warm when you want a simple reply.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "إِسْمَكَ / شْنُو".

too_formal.feedback: This is more formal than the conversational Yemeni pattern with "شْنُو".

exercises.tip: Question word first is very natural here: "شْنُو + إِسْمَكَ؟"

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm from Sana'a."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but adding "مَدِينَةِ" makes it sound more explicit and formal than needed.

exercises.tip: For cities and countries, "أَنَا مِنْ + place" is the basic everyday pattern.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أَنَا مِنْ عَدَن، _____ سَاكِنَة بِصَنْعَاء." Meaning: I'm from Aden, but I live in Sana'a.

too_formal.feedback: It is grammatical, but it is noticeably more formal than the everyday spoken connector "بِس".

exercises.tip: "بِس" is one of the most useful everyday words for "but".

exercises.prompt: Which reply fits "كَيْفَكَ؟" most naturally?

too_formal.feedback: That wording is far too formal for an ordinary spoken exchange.

exercises.tip: A simple health check usually gets a short answer: "تَمَام" or similar.

exercises.prompt: You are a man. Someone asks: "مِنْ وَيْن أَنْتَ؟" Say that you are from Sana'a.

too_formal.feedback: This is far more formal than a natural introduction.

exercises.tip: You can answer with the full sentence or simply "مِنْ صَنْعَاء" when the context is clear.

dialogue.speaker: Tareq
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: Yes, of course. What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Tareq
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: On the right, after the door.

pair.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

lessons.culture: In Yemeni speech, polite softeners such as "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ" and "مَعْلِش" are used frequently in everyday situations. A brief "شُكْرًا" followed by "عَفْوًا" is completely natural. The phrase "وَلَا يُهِمَّكَ" (no worries) is especially warm.

exercises.prompt: You need help from a man. Start politely with "Excuse me, can you help me?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Yemeni speech normally uses "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ" and "تِقْدِر".

exercises.tip: The spoken pattern is "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ + تِقْدِر...؟" when addressing a man.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Thank you very much."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic. "شُكْرًا كَتِير" is the natural conversational phrase.

exercises.tip: "كَتِير" can intensify thanks, praise, and many other everyday expressions.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ سَمَحْتَ، وَيْن الْحَمَّام؟"

too_formal.feedback: That wording is much more formal and uses a more formal term for bathroom.

exercises.tip: "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ" is a standard polite opener before a request.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase is a natural Yemeni way to say "You're welcome"?

too_formal.feedback: This is understandable, but it is more formulaic and formal than the simple everyday "عَفْوًا".

exercises.tip: "عَفْوًا" works very naturally as the reply to "شُكْرًا".

exercises.prompt: Someone says "شُكْرًا" to you. Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is polite but noticeably more formal and ceremonial than the everyday replies.

exercises.tip: "وَلَا يُهِمَّك" is especially conversational and warm.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want some water."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. Yemeni speech normally uses "بِدِّي" for "I want".

exercises.tip: "بِدِّي" is one of the core spoken patterns for wants and requests.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "Sorry" when the speaker is a man?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but it is more formal than the very common spoken "آسِف".

exercises.tip: The final vowel changes with the speaker's gender: "آسِف" for a man, "آسِفَة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Sorry, I didn't understand."

too_formal.feedback: That is formal Arabic. The spoken negative uses "مَا" here.

exercises.tip: In this kind of everyday past-tense statement, "مَا فَهِمْت" is the natural colloquial form.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in a natural order: "تِسَاعِدْنِي / تِقْدِر / لَوْ سَمَحْتَ".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than everyday Yemeni phrasing.

exercises.tip: Put the polite opener first, then the spoken ability pattern "تِقْدِر + verb".

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you politely for help and says "لَوْ سَمَحْتِ، تِقْدِرِي تِسَاعِدِينِي؟" Reply positively.

too_formal.feedback: This is warmer in a formal or service context, but it is much more elaborate than necessary in casual conversation.

exercises.tip: "إِي، أَكِيد" is an easy, friendly yes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reply: "شُكْرًا." — "_____ ."

too_formal.feedback: It is acceptable Arabic, but it is more formal and less direct than the everyday reply.

exercises.tip: Keep the reply short; native conversation often does.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "It's okay / Don't worry."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct but sounds more formal than the common spoken "مَعْلِش".

exercises.tip: "مَعْلِش" can soften a small apology, reassure someone, or excuse a minor inconvenience.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Samer
dialogue.english: Yes, I have a little work.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Good. Shall we see you tomorrow?

lessons.culture: In Yemeni casual speech, time is often discussed with simple whole-hour expressions rather than a full formal sentence. "بُكْرَة" and "الْآن" are especially common everyday words for planning and talking about the immediate future and present. Friday is the day of rest, and "الْجمُعَة" (Friday) is an important time marker.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What time is it?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but the colloquial Yemeni form usually uses just "الِسَّاعَة كَمْ؟"

exercises.tip: Use "كَمْ" for "how much/how many" in many everyday questions.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "It's two o'clock."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The spoken Yemeni number is commonly "اثْنَين" or similar.

exercises.tip: For casual speech, "اثْنَين" is a common spoken form of two.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "tomorrow"?

too_formal.feedback: This is standard formal Arabic; Yemeni speech uses "بُكْرَة".

exercises.tip: Remember the three basic time words: الْيَوْم, الْآن, بُكْرَة.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ فَاضِي." Meaning: I'm free tomorrow.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and more explicit than the everyday Yemeni sentence.

exercises.tip: Colloquial Arabic often lets the context make the pronoun clear.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "بُكْرَة فَاضِي؟" Reply that you are free.

too_formal.feedback: This is much more formal than a natural spoken answer.

exercises.tip: A short "إِي، فَاضِي" is enough when the question already gives the context.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Today I have a little work."

too_formal.feedback: This sounds like formal Arabic. Yemeni uses "عِنْدِي" and "شُغُل" in casual speech.

exercises.tip: "عِنْدِي" is the everyday way to express possession or something you have to do.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural sentence: "بُكْرَة / نِشُوفَكَ".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The spoken future here is built with "نِشُوفَكَ".

exercises.tip: In colloquial speech, future meaning is often built directly into the verb form.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Now"?

too_formal.feedback: This is understandable, but it is more formal than the everyday Yemeni "الْآن".

exercises.tip: "الْآن" is one of the most frequent everyday Yemeni time words.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "See you tomorrow." when speaking to a man.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The everyday Yemeni form uses "بِشُوفَكَ" or "نِشُوفَكَ".

exercises.tip: "بِشُوفَكَ" is a useful spoken phrase for saying that you will see someone.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الِسَّاعَة _____ مُنَاسِبَة؟" Meaning: Is one o'clock suitable?

too_formal.feedback: This is grammatical, but the short spoken form "الِسَّاعَة وَاحِدَة" is more natural.

exercises.tip: When telling the time, the spoken form often drops the formal case ending.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Three."

too_formal.feedback: This adds the article; for counting, just "ثَلَاثَة" is fine.

exercises.tip: Numbers are fairly standard across dialects.

exercises.prompt: Someone proposes meeting at one o'clock and asks if that works. Say yes.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and unnecessarily elaborate for a simple scheduling exchange.

exercises.tip: Use "مُنَاسِبَة" for a time that works for you.

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the market?

dialogue.speaker: Dima
dialogue.english: Yes, then you'll see it on the left.

lessons.culture: Giving directions in Sana'a is often conversational and incremental: a person may give one turn, wait for the listener to react, and then add the next step. "يَعْطِيكَ الْعَافِيَة" is a very common warm expression of thanks, especially after someone helps you. Markets (السُّوق) are central gathering places where people meet, shop, and socialize.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the market?"

too_formal.feedback: This is standard Arabic. "وَيْن السُّوق؟" is the natural colloquial Yemeni form.

exercises.tip: "وَيْن" is one of the first location words to learn for Yemeni conversation.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "On the right"?

too_formal.feedback: This is much more formal and explicit than the normal spoken direction.

exercises.tip: The preposition and noun are closely joined in speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Straight ahead."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and sounds like written instructions rather than everyday speech.

exercises.tip: "دُغْرِي" is an extremely useful conversational word for going straight.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "لُف _____ يَمِين." Meaning: Turn right.

too_formal.feedback: This is unnecessarily formal for a simple spoken direction.

exercises.tip: In speech, "عَلَى + يَمِينَك" is a common direction pattern.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks whether the market is far. Tell them it is very close.

too_formal.feedback: This uses formal vocabulary and structure; the everyday reply is much shorter.

exercises.tip: "كَتِير" often follows an adjective to make it stronger: "قَرِيب كَتِير".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Here."

too_formal.feedback: Both are understood, but "هُنَّا" is the standard everyday Yemeni form.

exercises.tip: Learn the pair "هُنَّا" for here and "هُنَاك" for there.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "there"?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal/classical; conversational Yemeni uses "هُنَاك".

exercises.tip: "هُنَاك" points to a place away from the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in a natural order: "السُّوق / وَيْن".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than the target colloquial pattern.

exercises.tip: A location question often starts with "وَيْن".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "And then?"

too_formal.feedback: That is formal and much longer than the normal spoken question.

exercises.tip: "بَعْدِين" is a very high-frequency conversational word meaning "then/later."

exercises.prompt: Someone thanks you with "يَعْطِيكَ الْعَافِيَة". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: That is not the usual conversational response to this fixed expression.

exercises.tip: Match the gender of the person you are addressing.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "Turn left" when speaking to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The everyday spoken imperative is "لُفِّي".

exercises.tip: The feminine imperative is "لُفِّي"; the masculine form is "لُف".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The market is near."

too_formal.feedback: The longer sentence is grammatical, but unnecessary when simply stating that the market is near.

exercises.tip: Simple adjective sentences can be very short in Yemeni Arabic.

challenge.title: Your First Yemeni Conversation
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Yemeni Arabic conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include a greeting, asking and answering names, asking where someone is from, one polite request, one thank-you exchange, one question about a time, and one set of directions. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 1 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A natural greeting using مَرْحَبًا, أَهْلًا, or أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا.
A name question and a name answer.
A question using مِنْ وَيْن and a place answer.
A polite request using لَوْ سَمَحْتَ or لَوْ سَمَحْتِ.
A response using إِي، أَكِيد or a natural equivalent.
A thank-you exchange using شُكْرًا and عَفْوًا or a natural equivalent.
A time question using الِسَّاعَة كَمْ؟
A future plan using بُكْرَة or a similar target expression.
At least two direction phrases such as عَلَى يَمِينَك, عَلَى شِمَالَك, دُغْرِي, هُنَّا, or هُنَاك.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أَهْلًا، تَمَام الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ. شْنُو إِسْمَكَ؟
dialogue.english: Hi, I'm fine, thank God. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: My name is Samer. And you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: I'm Lina. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.transliteration: w ana kiman. min wayn anti?
dialogue.english: Me too. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أَنَا مِنْ عَدَن، بِس سَاكِنَة بِصَنْعَاء.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min 3adan, bas sakna bi Sana2a.
dialogue.english: I'm from Aden, but I live in Sana'a.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Yes, of course. What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: مِنْ هُنَّا، إِمْشِ دُغْرِي وَبَعْدِين لُف عَلَى يَمِينَك.
dialogue.transliteration: min hunna, imshi dughri w ba3dain luff 3ala yaminek.
dialogue.english: From here, walk straight and then turn right.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: لَا، قَرِيب كَتِير. الِسَّاعَة كَمْ الْآن؟
dialogue.transliteration: la, qarib ktiir. is-sa3a kam il-aan?
dialogue.english: No, it's very close. What time is it now?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: تَمَام. بِشُوفَكَ بُكْرَة إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه.
dialogue.transliteration: tamaam. bishoofak bukra in sha2a allah.
dialogue.english: Good. See you tomorrow, God willing.
